rows.description: Displays OS build, architecture, kernel base, DTB and the symbol table that was resolved. Always the first command run — if this fails, no other plugin will work.
Searches the raw image for kernel banner strings. Fallback when windows.info fails or the dump type is unknown (also used to identify Linux images).
Lists the ISF (Intermediate Symbol Format) files available to Volatility and which images they match. The go-to fix for 'symbol table not found' errors.
Parses the header of a Windows crash dump (.dmp): build number, dump type, and physical memory run ranges.
Prints the KPCR structure for each processor. Confirms CPU count and gives kernel structure entry points used by other plugins.
Lists virtual mapped sections of kernel space (paged pool, PFN database, session space) — context for interpreting kernel addresses.
Walks the EPROCESS doubly-linked list to enumerate running processes (PID, PPID, image name, create/exit time, offset). Baseline of every investigation.
Pool-tag scans physical memory for EPROCESS objects independent of the linked list — surfaces terminated and DKOM-unlinked processes.
Renders parent/child hierarchy. Key for spotting abnormal ancestry (e.g. WINWORD.EXE -> powershell.exe, or services spawned by a user process).
Compares four independent process enumeration methods and flags any process missing from one of them — the classic anti-rootkit cross-view check.
Prints the command line of each process from the PEB. Reveals encoded PowerShell, LOLBin abuse, and dropped file paths.
Dumps environment variables per process — exposes injected paths, proxy settings, temp staging directories, and sometimes credentials.
Maps processes to their logon session and user, extracted from environment data. Distinguishes console, RDP, and service sessions.
Prints the SIDs owning each process — identifies privilege context and token-stealing (e.g. a user process running as SYSTEM).
Lists token privileges per process and whether each is enabled — flags SeDebugPrivilege or SeImpersonatePrivilege abuse.
Derives service SIDs and maps them to service names — links a token back to the service that owns it.
Prints job object links per process; useful for spotting sandboxed/containerised children and job-based process grouping.
Lists open handles per process (files, keys, mutexes, processes, tokens). Reveals malware mutexes, opened victim processes, and staged file paths.
Enumerates threads per process with start addresses — a start address outside any mapped module is a strong injection indicator.
Pool-scans for ETHREAD objects, including threads belonging to hidden or exited processes.
Lists threads in a suspended state — typical of process hollowing and injection before the payload is resumed.
Flags userland threads whose start address is unbacked, in a private region, or inconsistent with the owning module.
Lists DLLs loaded per process with their base addresses and full paths — reveals sideloaded, unsigned, or oddly-pathed modules.
Compares the three PEB module lists against the VAD tree; a module present in one but not the others indicates a manually mapped or unlinked DLL.
Extracts the IAT of a process image to enumerate imported APIs, and to detect IAT hooking or suspicious API surface.
Reads version resources from mapped PE files — spot forged company/product strings on masqueraded binaries.
Resolves symbols inside PE files in process and kernel memory — used to attribute unnamed addresses to real functions.
Lists every VAD (virtual address descriptor) with protection flags and backing file. PAGE_EXECUTE_READWRITE with no file is the injection signature.
Walks the raw VAD tree structure (parent/left/right nodes) — used to validate a tree that malfind or vadinfo could not parse cleanly.
Pool-scans for network objects: all active and closed connections for all processes, identifying foreign IPs, listening ports, owning PIDs, and timestamps. Works across all modern Windows builds.
Traverses the live network tracking structures instead of scanning. Fewer false positives than netscan, but misses closed connections.
Lists loaded registry hives with virtual/physical offsets. Provides the --offset value other registry plugins need.
Pool-scans for CMHIVE structures — finds hives unlinked from the list or belonging to unloaded user profiles.
Prints keys and values under a hive or path. The primary persistence check: Run, RunOnce, Services, Winlogon, IFEO.
Recursively walks every key and value under a hive or subkey — the Volatility 2 hivedump equivalent. Pipe to a file; output is large.
Decodes UserAssist entries — programs launched from Explorer with run counts and last-execution timestamps.
Parses the AmCache hive: executed binaries, full paths, SHA-1 hashes, and first-run timestamps. Strong execution evidence.
Reads Shimcache (AppCompatCache) entries from the ahcache.sys AVL tree in memory — file paths and timestamps of executed/present binaries.
Reports hives whose GetCellRoutine handler has been hooked — a rootkit technique to hide registry content from live tools.
Pool-scans for FILE_OBJECT structures. Identifies deleted and hidden files, timestamps (created/modified/accessed), full paths, and physical memory offsets of files referenced in memory.
Dumps cached file contents (DataSectionObject/ImageSectionObject) to disk. Use the offset from filescan, or --pid to grab a process's files.
Carves $MFT FILE records from memory: filenames, MACB timestamps, and resident attributes — timeline material without the disk image.
Extracts Alternate Data Streams from carved MFT records — a classic hiding place for payloads and download markers.
Recovers the content of small files stored resident inside MFT records — often scripts, configs, and notes.
Scans for and parses MBR structures in memory — detects bootkits and wiper-style MBR overwrites.
Scans for symbolic link objects in the object manager namespace — reveals device mappings and drive-letter abuse.
Prints the virtual-to-physical mapping of a process and, with --dump, writes the full process address space to disk.
Rebuilds and writes each listed process image to disk — the Volatility 2 procdump equivalent. Scope with --pid or you will dump every process.
Writes listed DLLs to disk — the Volatility 2 dlldump equivalent. --name filters by regex; fails if the PE header page is not resident.
Writes selected VAD regions to disk — the Volatility 2 vaddump equivalent, and the fallback when header-based dumping fails. --maxsize caps huge regions.
Writes kernel drivers to disk — the Volatility 2 moddump equivalent. --base extracts a single driver by address.
Extracts exactly the regions malfind flagged, one file per VAD — the fastest path from detection to a sample you can analyse.
Searches for cached TrueCrypt passphrases and keys left in memory by the driver.
Finds private, committed VADs marked executable with no backing file, and hexdumps/disassembles the head — shellcode and injected PE headers (MZ) show up here.
Runs YARA rules across the entire memory image (kernel and user space). Broadest signature sweep; use for known-malware or flag-string hunting.
Runs YARA only against process VADs, so every hit maps to a PID and region — far more actionable than a raw-image hit.
Regex search across process memory regions — good for URLs, base64 blobs, wallet addresses, and CTF flag patterns.
Compares the on-disk PE backing a process against its in-memory image to detect hollowing/replacement of legitimate binaries.
Flags processes whose backing FILE_OBJECT is deleted, null, or delete-on-close — the ghosting/doppelgänging family of techniques.
Compares the image path in EPROCESS against the PEB — catches malware that rewrites its own PEB to impersonate a system binary.
Detects ntdll.dll stubs that differ from the clean on-disk version — the signature of userland EDR unhooking.
Finds syscall stubs executed outside ntdll (Hell's Gate / SysWhispers style) used to bypass userland hooks.
Detects the indirect-syscall variant where the syscall instruction is borrowed from ntdll but reached from foreign code.
Identifies patched ETW functions (e.g. EtwEventWrite) used to blind telemetry before executing payloads.
Inspects thread debug registers (DR0-DR7) — hardware breakpoints are used both by anti-analysis code and by hooking frameworks.
Rebuilds and dumps a PE file from a given base address in process or kernel space — how you recover the payload for static analysis.
Walks PsLoadedModuleList to list loaded kernel drivers with base addresses and paths.
Pool-scans for kernel modules independent of the list — modules present here but absent from windows.modules are hidden.
Lists recently unloaded drivers with unload timestamps — evidence of a rootkit that loaded, acted, and removed itself.
Pool-scans for DRIVER_OBJECT structures, including drivers unlinked from the standard list.
Correlates driver objects with kernel modules to prove a driver is hidden — a driver object with no matching module is a rootkit indicator.
Lists the IRP dispatch table of each driver; handlers pointing outside the owning driver's range indicate IRP hooking.
Renders drivers and their attached devices as a tree — reveals filter drivers inserted into the keyboard, disk, or network stack.
Dumps the System Service Descriptor Table and resolves each entry to its owning module; entries outside ntoskrnl/win32k are hooks.
Lists kernel notification routines (process/thread/image load, registry callbacks) — both a rootkit persistence point and an EDR footprint.
Prints kernel timers and their associated DPC routines with owning module — a stealth execution path for kernel implants.
Finds kernel threads whose start address maps to no loaded module — code running from unbacked kernel memory.
Lists big page pool allocations with tags — oversized or oddly-tagged allocations often hold kernel payloads.
Framework-level pool scanner used by the other *scan plugins; can be pointed at arbitrary tags for custom hunting.
Scans for mutant (mutex) objects. Malware families use hardcoded mutex names as single-instance markers — excellent IOC pivot.
Extracts local account NTLM hashes from the SAM and SYSTEM hives in memory — evidence of, or material for, credential attacks.
Decrypts LSA secrets from the SECURITY hive: service account passwords, cached machine secrets, DPAPI keys.
Dumps cached domain credential hashes (MSCache/DCC2) for users who logged in without a reachable DC.
Checks lsass for the Skeleton Key patch, which lets an attacker authenticate as any domain user with a master password.

Scans service records: name, display name, type, state, and binary path. Identifies malicious or suspicious service configurations, modified service paths, unverified distributors, and anomalous network-triggering services; paths in temp or user directories are prime persistence findings.
Enumerates services by walking the service record list rather than scanning — the clean baseline for comparison.
Diffs list-walked services against scanned services; anything only visible to the scanner is a service hidden by a rootkit.
Decodes scheduled tasks from the registry: actions, triggers, principals, and hidden-flag state. Top-tier persistence artifact.
Recovers the command history buffers of cmd.exe (COMMAND_HISTORY), including commands typed and then cleared.
Recovers full console input and output buffers — you get the attacker's commands together with the output they saw.
Scans for top-level window stations — the GUI containers used for session isolation and desktop hiding.
Lists desktop instances per window station; malware creates hidden desktops to run GUI apps invisibly.
Enumerates windows belonging to desktop instances, including titles — recovers what was on screen and by which process.
Takes output from the strings utility and maps each offset back to the owning process and virtual address — turns a raw string hit into a lead.
rows.command: strings -td mem.raw > s.txt; vol -f mem.raw windows.strings --strings-file s.txt

rows.description: Aggregates timestamps from every plugin that produces them into one chronological timeline. Best single command for 'what happened, in order'.
Writes the primary memory layer out to a flat raw file — converts crash dumps, VMware, and hibernation images into raw for other tools.
Extracts kernel banner strings from the image (distro, kernel version, build date, compiler). Mandatory first step: the banner tells you exactly which ISF symbol file you must build or download.
Lists the ISF files Volatility can see and which banners they match. Use it to confirm your generated symbol file is actually being picked up.
Reports when the system was started — anchors every other timestamp and lets you compute uptime at capture.
Enumerates VMCOREINFO tables embedded in the image: kernel offsets, KASLR base, and structure sizes. Useful when symbols only partially resolve.
Enumerates kernel symbols from the in-memory kallsyms table, including symbols from loaded modules. Ground truth for validating addresses seen elsewhere.
Reproduces /proc/iomem — the physical address map of system RAM and device regions.
Walks the task_struct linked list to enumerate running tasks (PID, TID, PPID, COMM, UID/GID, offset). Baseline process view.
Scans memory for task_struct signatures independently of the linked list — reveals processes unlinked by a rootkit.
Enumerates tasks through the kernel PID hash table — a third, independent view. Cross-compare with pslist and psscan for hidden tasks.
Renders the parent/child hierarchy. Catches shells spawned by web servers, cron-spawned implants, and reparented daemons.
Reconstructs full argv per task, like ps aux — exposes reverse-shell one-liners, curl-pipe-bash, and encoded payload arguments.
Dumps environment variables per process. LD_PRELOAD, HTTP_PROXY, and credentials passed via env show up here.
Lists the capability sets of each task (permitted, effective, inheritable, bounding). CAP_SYS_ADMIN or CAP_SYS_MODULE on an odd process is a privilege-escalation lead.
Compares each task's executable path against its cmdline and comm fields — catches implants masquerading as kernel threads or system daemons.
Enumerates kernel threads and their entry functions — a kthread whose function is not in a legitimate module is a kernel implant.
Lists ptrace tracer/tracee relationships — reveals injection via ptrace and anti-debug self-tracing.
Reconstructs the kernel call stack of each task; frames resolving to unknown addresses indicate execution from hidden modules.
Lists VMAs per process, like /proc/pid/maps: address range, permissions, and backing file. The Linux equivalent of vadinfo.
Lists every memory-mapped ELF per process; --dump rebuilds them to disk for static analysis.
Lists shared objects loaded into each process — detects LD_PRELOAD hijacks and trojanised .so files.
Enumerates sockets per task (TCP/UDP/UNIX/netlink) with local/remote addresses, state, and owning PID. Primary C2 and backdoor discovery plugin.
Scans the memory layer for socket structures independent of the task list — finds sockets belonging to hidden or exited processes.
Lists network interfaces and their addresses, like ip addr show — including promiscuous-mode flags that suggest sniffing.
Lists link-layer interface details, like ip link show — reveals unexpected tunnels, taps, and bridges.
Lists registered netfilter (iptables/nftables) hook functions; hooks owned by unknown modules are used for traffic hiding, redirection, or port-knocking triggers.
Compares each syscall table entry against its expected symbol; anything pointing outside the kernel text is a hooked syscall.
Verifies the Interrupt Descriptor Table against known-good handlers — detects low-level interrupt hooking.
Verifies af_inet/af_inet6 operation structures; hooked TCP/UDP handlers are used to hide connections from netstat-like tools.
Compares the kernel module list against sysfs — a module in one and not the other has been unlinked to hide itself.
Detects processes sharing a cred structure — the fingerprint of a rootkit granting root to a chosen process.
Checks tty receive_buf function pointers for hooks — the standard kernel keylogger technique.
Parses the keyboard notifier call chain; unexpected callbacks are keyloggers registered as notifiers.
Detects function hooking implemented via the ftrace framework — the modern, stealthy successor to syscall table patching.
Detects handlers attached to kernel tracepoints, another legitimate subsystem abused for stealth hooking.
Lists perf events per process; attacker-registered events can capture data or execute callbacks without a module.
Enumerates loaded eBPF programs and maps — increasingly the payload of choice for modern Linux rootkits and stealth C2.
Lists open file descriptors per process (files, sockets, pipes, deleted files) with inode metadata — finds staged payloads and open exfil handles.
Lists mount points per mount namespace — exposes container boundaries, bind mounts of host paths, and escape indicators.
Lists files present in the kernel page cache, with paths and inode details — the Linux equivalent of filescan.
Lists and dumps the cached pages of a specific inode — recovers file content, including deleted files still cached in RAM.
Recovers the entire cached filesystem tree (files, directories, symlinks) into a compressed tarball. Heavy, but often yields the whole attacker toolkit.
Finds VMAs with write+execute permissions and no backing file — injected shellcode and unpacked payloads in process memory.
Runs YARA rules across the whole image, kernel space included. Broadest sweep for known malware strings and flag patterns.
Runs YARA against process VMAs so each hit maps to a PID and region — the actionable version of a raw-image hit.
Regex search across process VMAs — URLs, IPs, key material, and CTF flag formats.
Lists modules from the standard module list, with taint flags — the clean baseline for hidden-module comparison.
Carves module structures out of memory and reports those absent from the standard list — LKM rootkits that unlinked themselves.
Merges lsmod, check_modules, and hidden_modules into one table with taint state — the fastest single command for module-level rootkit triage.
Rebuilds an ELF module from a kernel address to disk — how you recover a hidden LKM for reverse engineering.
Extracts in-memory bash history buffers with timestamps — direct evidence of the commands an attacker typed, including history never written to disk.
Reads the kernel ring buffer (dmesg) — module loads, OOM kills, segfaults, and USB/device events around the incident.
Extracts framebuffer content from the fbdev subsystem — recovers what was rendered on the console screen.
With --dump, writes selected VMAs to disk — the extraction step after malfind or a YARA hit identifies a region.
With --dump, rebuilds mapped ELF images to disk, including deleted binaries still resident in memory.
Rebuilds a kernel module ELF from its base address — the extraction step after modxview or hidden_modules names an address.
Writes the primary memory layer to a flat raw file — converts LiME, AVML, and crash formats for use with other tooling.
Aggregates timestamps from every timestamp-producing Linux plugin into one chronological view — process starts, bash history, file metadata.
Regex search across the entire image regardless of process context — the catch-all when a scoped scan finds nothing.
Writes the resolved configuration (layers, symbols, offsets) to JSON — makes a long analysis reproducible and shareable.

windows_workflow.objectives: Confirm the image is parseable, identify OS build and architecture, and verify the correct symbol table loaded before anything else is trusted.
Establish the process baseline, then attack it from multiple angles: hidden/unlinked processes, spoofed lineage, injected threads, unlinked DLLs, and RWX memory regions.
Recover active, closed, and listening endpoints; map outbound C2 (Command & Control) IP addresses and listening backdoors back to a specific PID and process image.
Read persistence keys (Run, Services, Winlogon, IFEO), recover execution evidence from AmCache/Shimcache/UserAssist, and detect registry-level rootkit hooks.
Locate and extract files still resident in memory, recover MFT records and ADS for timeline building, and dump process address spaces for offline analysis.
Hunt injected and unbacked code, hollowed and ghosted processes, spoofed PEBs, EDR evasion via syscalls and ETW patching, and signature matches via YARA.
Detect kernel-mode compromise: hidden drivers and modules, SSDT/IRP hooks, malicious callbacks and timers, and code executing from unbacked kernel memory.
Extract NTLM hashes, LSA secrets, and cached domain credentials, and check for domain-level backdoors such as Skeleton Key.
Audit services and scheduled tasks for abnormal binary paths, hidden entries visible only to scanning, and attacker-created autostart mechanisms.
Recover typed commands and console output, reconstruct on-screen activity, attribute raw strings to processes, and build a unified timeline of the incident.

linux_workflow.objectives: Identify the exact kernel build from the banner and confirm a matching ISF symbol file is loading — on Linux, no symbols means no analysis at all.
Build the task baseline from three independent enumeration paths, then check argv, environment, capabilities, name spoofing, and mapped ELFs for anomalies.
Enumerate sockets per task and by scanning, review interface state for sniffing, and inspect netfilter hooks used to hide or redirect traffic.
Test every classic and modern kernel hook point: syscall table, IDT, protocol handlers, credentials, TTY, notifiers, ftrace, tracepoints, perf, and eBPF.
Recover open descriptors, mount and namespace layout for container context, and pull cached file content — up to the entire cached filesystem — out of RAM.
Find injected RWX regions, match YARA signatures inside process memory, and resolve module-level rootkits by cross-viewing lsmod against carved structures.
Recover attacker-typed commands from in-memory bash history, read the kernel log for module loads and crashes, and recover console framebuffer content.
Extract the artifacts you found: specific VMAs, mapped and deleted ELF binaries, hidden kernel modules, and a flat raw copy of the memory layer.
Assemble a chronological account of the incident and preserve a reproducible configuration of how the image was parsed.

framework.description: Scans the image for kernel banner strings. Identifies Linux kernels and confirms Windows images when info plugins fail.
Reports available ISF symbol files and which images they match. First stop for symbol resolution failures.
YARA scanning across the full memory image, independent of OS and process context.
Regex scanning across the full image — useful for flags, URLs, emails, and key material.
Aggregates timestamps from all timestamp-producing plugins into one sortable timeline.
Writes the primary memory layer to a flat raw file — format conversion for third-party tools.
Exports the resolved analysis configuration (layers, symbols, offsets) as JSON for reproducibility.
Lists the framework's own components: layers, symbol tables, automagic modules, and available plugins.

Not a plugin — a second entry point shipped beside vol.py. Drops you into a Python shell with the image loaded so you can walk structures directly (ps(), dt('_EPROCESS'), db(addr)). This is how you answer questions no plugin covers.
Scans for virtual machine host/guest structures inside a hypervisor memory image (nested memory analysis).

triage.look_for: Processes with 0 threads, 0 handles, or a populated Exit time
triage.why: They are terminated but still linked in the active list. Not a rootkit finding — a common false lead for beginners.

triage.look_for: System (PID 4) and smss.exe with no Session ID
triage.why: Expected, not an anomaly: System starts before sessions exist and smss.exe is the session manager itself.

triage.look_for: Processes present in psscan but absent from pslist
triage.why: Either terminated, or unlinked from the EPROCESS list by DKOM. Check the Exit time before calling it a rootkit.

triage.look_for: Processes in pslist but not psscan
triage.why: Usually pool memory reuse or a scanning miss — the list view is generally the more reliable of the two for live processes.

triage.look_for: svchost.exe whose parent is not services.exe, or with no -k argument in its command line
triage.why: The single highest-yield Windows anomaly. Legitimate svchost is always services-spawned and always has a -k service group.

triage.look_for: csrss.exe and wininit.exe showing a PPID that no longer exists
triage.why: Normal: their parent smss.exe exits after boot. Orphaned PPID alone is not suspicious for these.

triage.look_for: Office, browser, or Acrobat processes with a shell or script host child
triage.why: WINWORD.EXE spawning powershell.exe, cmd.exe or wscript.exe is the classic initial-access pattern.

triage.look_for: A system binary name running from anywhere other than System32 or SysWOW64
triage.why: Masquerading is cheap and common. Always compare the path, not just the process name.

triage.look_for: PAGE_NOACCESS in vadinfo output
triage.why: vadinfo reports the ORIGINAL protection from the first allocation, not the current one. A region shown as NOACCESS may still be executable now.

triage.look_for: RWX private VADs containing an MZ header
triage.why: An injected PE. Regions with no MZ but valid-looking instructions are shellcode — disassemble before concluding.

triage.look_for: Dozens of RWX hits in browsers, .NET, or Java processes
triage.why: JIT compilers allocate RWX legitimately. malfind is a lead generator, not a verdict; correlate with thread start addresses and module backing.

triage.look_for: A Wow64 process showing very few DLLs
triage.why: The PEB lists are truncated for Wow64. Use windows.malware.ldrmodules instead of dlllist for 32-bit processes on 64-bit systems.

triage.look_for: Thread start addresses that map to no loaded module
triage.why: Stronger evidence than malfind alone: code executing from unbacked memory. windows.malware.suspicious_threads automates this check.

triage.look_for: Endpoints whose owning PID does not appear in any process listing
triage.why: Either a hidden process or a stale pool artifact. netscan is a scanner, so corrupt and historical entries are expected.

triage.look_for: netscan returning nothing on a busy system
triage.why: Try --include-corrupt to relax validation, and cross-check with windows.netstat, which walks live structures instead.

triage.look_for: cmdscan showing fewer commands than expected
triage.why: The default MaxHistory is 50 and is user-configurable via HKCU\Console\HistoryBufferSize. Use --max-history and prefer consoles, which returns output as well as input.

triage.look_for: Unusual named mutexes
triage.why: Malware families use hardcoded mutex names as single-instance markers — one of the best pivots from a memory image to threat-intel attribution.

triage.look_for: Any *scan plugin result
triage.why: Scanners find objects in pool memory that may be freed, reused, or partially overwritten. A hit proves the object existed at some point, not that it was live at capture time.

triage.look_for: Dumping fails with a paged-out header
triage.why: If the page holding the PE header is not resident, pedump and dlllist --dump fail. Fall back to vadinfo --dump and rebuild the header manually.

triage.look_for: All plugin timestamps
triage.why: Volatility reports UTC. Reconcile against the system time zone before building a timeline or correlating with logs.

triage.look_for: Structures that contradict each other
triage.why: A dump taken over minutes on a live system is not an atomic snapshot. Smear produces genuinely inconsistent structures — do not force a rootkit narrative onto it.

triage.look_for: Plugins returning empty tables rather than errors
triage.why: A near-match ISF file is worse than none: offsets resolve to garbage and output looks plausible but is wrong. Confirm the banner matches your symbol file exactly.

triage.look_for: Bracketed names in pslist output
triage.why: Those are kernel threads. Use --decorate-comm to distinguish kernel threads and user threads before treating one as anomalous.

triage.look_for: lsmod output that looks clean
triage.why: Clean lsmod means nothing on its own — it is the list a rootkit unlinks from. Run linux.malware.modxview to compare it against carved and sysfs views in one table.

notes.notes: Volatility 3 plugin names are namespaced and case-sensitive. The entry point is `vol` (or `python3 vol.py`). Use `vol -h` for global options and `vol <plugin> -h` for plugin-specific ones.
The full plugin list for your installed version is printed at the bottom of `vol -h`. Plugin sets differ between versions — always check against your own install rather than a cheat sheet.

As of Volatility 3 v2.2x, malware-detection plugins moved into `.malware` subpackages. The old top-level names (windows.malfind, linux.check_syscall, ...) still work but print a deprecation warning. This sheet uses the new names.
Windows symbol tables are downloaded automatically from the Microsoft symbol server on first use. A failure here almost always means no network access or an unsupported build.

Linux requires an ISF file built from the exact kernel's debug symbols (`dwarf2json linux --elf vmlinux > kernel.json`), placed in `volatility3/symbols/linux/`. No matching ISF means every Linux plugin fails.
`-r csv` is the fastest way to get plugin output into a spreadsheet or grep pipeline; `-r json` for scripting. Add `-q` to suppress progress output.
The output directory flag `-o` is global and comes before the plugin name. Plugins that write files (dumpfiles, pedump, memmap, elfs, module_extract) need it.
Most process plugins accept `--pid`. Scope early: running dlllist or handles across every process on a busy image is slow and noisy.
`*scan` plugins brute-force the physical layer and are slow but see hidden objects; list-walking plugins are fast but trust kernel structures a rootkit may have edited. Run both and diff them.
Volatility 3 also ships a macOS plugin set (mac.pslist, mac.netstat, mac.malfind, ...). It is out of scope for this workbook and rarely used in CTF challenges.

Some plugins are hidden if a dependency is missing: yarascan/vadyarascan/vmayarascan/mftscan need yara-python, the hashdump/lsadump/cachedump family needs pycryptodome, and the direct/indirect syscall plugins need capstone. If a plugin here is 'not found', install the dependency before assuming your version lacks it.

The CLI accepts a shortened plugin name (windows.pslist) as long as it is unambiguous. Ambiguous prefixes are rejected: use windows.windows.Windows, since windows.windows also prefixes windows.windowstations.
Rules are passed with --yara-string (inline), --yara-file (a .yar file), or --yara-compiled-file. Add --wide for UTF-16 strings and --insensitive for case-insensitive matching.

Interactive structure exploration. -w / -l / -m select Windows, Linux or Mac mode; --pid sets process context. Inside: hh() for help, ps() to list processes, cc(pid=N) to change context, dt() to display a structure type, db()/dd() to dump bytes. The fastest way to learn what a plugin is actually doing.

Almost every public walkthrough uses Volatility 2 syntax with --profile=. The 'Volatility 2 to 3 Translation' sheet in this workbook maps the old commands, and flags the ones with no Volatility 3 equivalent.
Plugin names and descriptions in this workbook were verified against the Volatility 3 stable branch, version 2.28. Older installs will lack some plugins listed here.
